title: Fix JsonRequest.replace ignoring replacement dumps_kwargs
body:
﻿Fixes #8493

### Root Cause
`JsonRequest.replace()` serialized `data` using `self._dumps(data)` (which reads `self._dumps_kwargs`) before delegating to `super().replace()`, so replacement `dumps_kwargs` passed to `replace(data=..., dumps_kwargs=...)` were stored on the returned request but ignored during JSON serialization of `data`.

### Changes
- Extract `_normalize_dumps_kwargs()` in `scrapy/http/request/json_request.py` and use it in both `__init__()` and `replace()`.
- Update `_dumps()` to accept optional `dumps_kwargs` and pass normalized replacement `dumps_kwargs` (including `dumps_kwargs=None`) from `replace()` when `"dumps_kwargs" in kwargs`.
- Add regression tests in `tests/test_http_request_json.py` covering replacement `dumps_kwargs`, `dumps_kwargs=None` reset behavior, and preservation of the original request's `dumps_kwargs` and `body`.

### Verification
- `pytest tests/test_http_request_json.py tests/test_request_dict.py` (68 passed)

title: Support common curl options in Request.from_curl (-A, -e, -x, -G, --data-binary, --json)
body:
Closes #8427

## What changed

`Request.from_curl()` treated several common curl options as unknown, so their values were parsed as the positional URL (the real URL was dropped) or the option silently changed/dropped parts of the request. In `scrapy/utils/curl.py`:

- `-A`/`--user-agent` now sets the `User-Agent` header and `-e`/`--referer` the `Referer` header (an explicit `-H` for the same header still wins, as in curl).
- `-x`/`--proxy` now sets `meta={"proxy": ...}` instead of becoming the URL.
- `--data-binary` is accepted as a data option with the same behavior as `--data-raw`.
- `--json` now sends its body, defaulting the method to POST and adding `Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: application/json` unless already given via `-H` (curl's documented `--json` behavior).
- `-G`/`--get` appends the `-d` data to the URL query string and keeps the GET method (unless `-X` says otherwise) instead of sending a POST body.
- An `-H` HTTP/2 pseudo-header such as `:authority: example.com` (included by Firefox and other tools when copying as cURL) no longer produces a header with an empty name; it is dropped, since it is not a real header.

Every example from #8427 now converts the way curl behaves; still-unknown options keep the existing warn-or-raise behavior.

title: Stream file contents when persisting to filesystem and GCS stores
body:
Closes #8410

## What changed

The persist paths of the filesystem and GCS files stores materialized a second full in-memory copy of every downloaded file via `buf.getvalue()`, doubling peak memory for the whole (slow) write/upload:

- `FSFilesStore.persist_file`: rewinds the buffer and streams it to disk with `shutil.copyfileobj` instead of `absolute_path.write_bytes(buf.getvalue())`.
- `GCSFilesStore.persist_file`: rewinds the buffer and calls `blob.upload_from_file(file_obj=buf, ...)` instead of `blob.upload_from_string(data=buf.getvalue(), ...)`; `content_type`, `predefined_acl` and `timeout` are passed exactly as before.

No caller changes are needed; both buffers are `BytesIO` at these callsites.

## Verification

- New regression test `TestFSFilesStore.test_persist_file_streams_without_copying` persists a `BytesIO` subclass whose `getvalue()` raises, and asserts the bytes on disk are identical. The three GCS persist tests now assert `upload_from_file` receives the stream object itself (with the uploaded content checked) instead of a `bytes` copy.
- Without this change, those 4 tests fail; with it, they pass.
- Full `tests/test_pipeline_files.py`: 90 passed, 28 skipped (the skips are the optional S3/botocore and similar surfaces not installed here).

title: Support more curl options in Request.from_curl()
body:
Resolves #8427

`Request.from_curl()` only knew a handful of curl options. A value-taking option it did not know was reported as unrecognized, but its value was still consumed as the `url` positional argument, so the resulting request went to the wrong URL (for example the proxy address passed to `-x`). Other common options were silently dropped.

Supported now:

- `-A`/`--user-agent` and `-e`/`--referer` set the corresponding headers. An explicit `-H` header wins over the option value.
- `-x`/`--proxy` sets `meta["proxy"]`.
- `--data-binary` and `--data-ascii` work like `--data-raw`.
- `--json` sends the given data as the body and sets `Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: application/json`, unless those headers are given with `-H`.
- `-G`/`--get` appends the data to the URL query string and keeps the method GET.
- `-I`/`--head` produces a HEAD request.

Headers whose name starts with `:` (HTTP/2 pseudo-headers such as `:authority`, which some browsers add when copying a request as cURL) are skipped instead of producing a header with an empty name.

Truly unknown options that take a value (for example `--max-time 5`) can still take the place of the URL; picking the URL among several positional arguments needs a heuristic, so I left that part out of this PR.

title: Do not warn about requests built by get_retry_request()
body:
## Summary

Fixes #8447. `get_retry_request()` is meant to be called from spider callbacks, and it copies the request it retries, meta included. When that request is `response.request`, its meta is `response.meta`, so the retry carries `download_latency`, `cache_timestamp`, `retry_times` and, after a redirect or through a proxy, the redirect and proxy keys, all on purpose. `MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware` could not tell such a retry from a spider copying `response.meta` into a new request, and warned.

## Fix

`get_retry_request()` now records the requests it builds in a private `WeakSet` in `scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry`, and `MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware` skips those exact objects. Nothing is added to the request meta. A request built from a retry (e.g. with `.replace()`), or with copied meta, is still checked, and skipping a retry does not use up the single warning of the crawl. The middleware docs mention the exception.

## Alternatives considered

- Dropping keys in `get_retry_request()` (the approach of #8448) is not enough on its own: a retry also legitimately carries `redirect_*`, `_auth_proxy` and `_scheme_proxy` from the request it retries.
- A heuristic in the middleware (from @hamarshehmhmd's analysis on the issue, thanks!): treat a request as a retry if it has the same URL, method and body and `retry_times` is one higher. That works without touching `retry.py`, but it is a guess; marking the actual objects is exact and also keeps marker keys out of user-visible meta, which was the concern raised there about a meta marker.

## Test plan

- 4 new tests in `tests/test_spidermiddleware_metacopy.py`: a retry of a response with download, cache and redirect keys does not warn; a second retry does not warn; a copied-meta request yielded after a retry still warns; a request built from a retry still warns. The first 3 fail on `master`.
- A real crawl with a spider retrying twice from its callback warns on `master` and does not with the change.
- tox: `pre-commit`, `mypy`, `mypy-tests`, `pylint` and `docs-tests` pass. Spider and downloader middleware, engine and crawl tests: 1661 passed, 20 skipped, 86 xfailed.

## Note, not addressed here

A retry that bypasses the cache (e.g. with `dont_cache`) may keep a stale `cache_timestamp`, because `HttpCacheMiddleware` does not clear it on a firsthand download. Not verified.

`CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` documents `0` as "no limit", but setting `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 0` (or `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP = 0` with the per-domain setting also 0) hangs the crawl: `Slot.free_transfer_slots()` returns `0 - len(transferring)`, which never goes above 0, so `_process_queue()` never sends any request (as diagnosed in #8449).

Fixes #8449.

## Changes
- `Slot.free_transfer_slots()` returns "one more free slot" whenever `concurrency` is 0, mirroring how `needs_backout()` already treats `total_concurrency == 0` as no limit. `_process_queue`'s `while` loop then drains the queue naturally, bounded by the global `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` backout.
- Documented `0` = no limit for `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN` (matches the existing wording used for `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS`).
- Added `test_free_transfer_slots` covering both the regular and the 0/unlimited cases (7 new parametrized cases; whole file 14 passed).

## Verification (2026-11-03, on origin/master e397746)
- `pytest tests/test_downloaderslotssettings.py` → 14 passed
- `pytest tests/test_engine.py tests/test_downloadermiddleware.py tests/test_scheduler.py` → 93 passed
- `ruff check` on both touched Python files → clean

title: Avoid buffering a second full copy when persisting files in FilesPipeline
body:
Avoid buffering a second full copy of every downloaded file when persisting it.

`FSFilesStore.persist_file` used `write_bytes(buf.getvalue())` and `GCSFilesStore.persist` used `upload_from_string(data=buf.getvalue())`, both of which materialize the whole buffer a second time and peak at ~2x the file size for the entire (slow) disk write / upload. Closes #8410

title: Fix #8419: Key RobotsTxtMiddleware parsers by scheme and netloc
body:
Resolves #8419.

I have read the [contributing guide](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html) and [set up pre-commit](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html#pre-commit).

### Description
In `RobotsTxtMiddleware`, the internal parser dictionary `self._parsers` was previously keyed solely by `netloc`. Requests to `http://host:port` and `https://host:port` consequently collided on the same cache key and shared a single parser, violating [RFC 9309 Section 2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309#section-2.3).

### Changes
- Updated `self._parsers` keying to origin key `f"{url.scheme}://{url.netloc}"`.
- Updated helper methods `_parse_robots` and `_robots_error` to use this origin key.
- Added unit test `test_robotstxt_scheme_isolation` in `tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py` verifying that HTTP and HTTPS schemes for the same authority maintain isolated parsers and download respective robots.txt files.

title: Do not copy download_latency and cache_timestamp on retry
body:
`get_retry_request()` copies the original request, so the new request inherited `download_latency` and `cache_timestamp`, even though both describe the download that had just finished. title: Do not overwrite the last stored feed batch when resuming a crawl
body:
When a crawl is resumed with `JOBDIR`, feed batches restart from the batch that was in progress when the previous run stopped, but that batch was already stored on close if it had any items. The resumed run then writes it again: with the `overwrite` mode (the default for S3, GCS and FTP) its items are lost, with `create` the new items are dropped as a conflict, and with `append` (the default for local files) a JSON batch ends up holding two arrays. title: Fix RobotsTxtMiddleware sharing rules across schemes with same authority
body:
Resolves #8419.

### Description
Under [RFC 9309 §2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309#section-2.3), robots.txt directives are defined for the combination of URI scheme and authority (`scheme://authority/robots.txt`).

Previously, `RobotsTxtMiddleware` cached robots parsers in `self._parsers` using `url.netloc`. When requests to `http://example.com` and `https://example.com` were processed by the spider, they mistakenly shared the same robots parser. If the HTTP site permitted a path while the HTTPS site disallowed it, fetching HTTP first would cause subsequent HTTPS requests to bypass the HTTPS robots exclusion policy.

This change:
- Keys `self._parsers` by origin (`f"{url.scheme}://{url.netloc}"`) so HTTP and HTTPS maintain isolated robots parsers.
- Introduces helper `_parser_key(request)` and updates `_is_robotstxt_request` accordingly.
- Adds regression tests in `tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py` ensuring scheme isolation between HTTP and HTTPS requests targeting the same authority.

title: Decode escapes in Bash $'...' strings in from_curl
body:
Resolves #8426.

`_normalize_curl_command` turned Bash `$'...'` strings into plain `'...'` strings, so the escapes inside them were passed through literally (`\n` stayed as backslash plus `n`), and a `\'` escape, which "Copy as cURL (bash)" emits for apostrophes, made `shlex` fail with "No closing quotation".

Now each `$'...'` string is found (honouring backslash escapes), decoded following the [Bash ANSI-C quoting rules](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/ANSI_002dC-Quoting.html) (`\a \b \e \E \f \n \r \t \v \\ \' \" \?`, `\nnn`, `\xHH`, `\uHHHH`, `\UHHHHHHHH`, `\cX`; unknown escapes are kept as is), and re-quoted with `shlex.quote` before splitting. `\xHH`/`\nnn` produce raw bytes like in Bash, so `$'\xc3\xa9'` becomes `é`. An unterminated `$'` keeps the old behaviour so `shlex` still reports it.

I compared the decoded output with `printf '%s' $'...'` in Bash for the cases in the tests.

Tests: 3 new tests in `tests/test_utils_curl.py` (escapes, escaped apostrophe, numeric escapes) fail on master and pass with this change; `pytest tests/test_utils_curl.py tests/test_http_request.py -k curl`, `ruff check`, `ruff format` and `mypy scrapy/utils/curl.py` pass.

title: Fall back to the settings policy on a bad referrer_policy import path in meta
body:
### Problem
`RefererMiddleware.policy()` documents that "if the policy is set in meta but is wrong (e.g. a typo error), the policy from settings is used", and the `unknown-meta-*` tests cover that for policy names. For an import path, though, `_load_policy_class()` only catches `ValueError` from `load_object()`, which raises `ImportError` for a mistyped module and `NameError` for a mistyped class name. So `Request(url, meta={"referrer_policy": "myproject.policies.Custm"})` raises out of the spider middleware, and the rest of the callback's output (items and requests after that request) is lost.

### Change
In `_load_policy_class()`, catch `ImportError`/`NameError` from `load_object()`. With `warning_only=True` (the meta and header path), emit the same "Could not load referrer policy" `RuntimeWarning`, with the underlying error appended, and return `None`, so the settings policy is used. With `warning_only=False` (the `REFERRER_POLICY` setting), the original exception is re-raised, so that behaviour is unchanged.

One trade-off: if a custom policy in meta that is stricter than the settings policy fails to import, the request now uses the settings policy and only warns. That's the same thing that already happens for a mistyped policy name.

title: Fix OffsiteMiddleware domain matching to be case-insensitive
body:
Fix `OffsiteMiddleware` domain matching to be case-insensitive.

## Description

`re.escape(domain)` in `get_host_regex` did not normalize to lowercase, while `urlparse(...).hostname` is always lowercase. A spider configured with:

```python
allowed_domains = ["Example.COM"]
```

would silently filter **every** request as offsite (the regex `Example\.COM` never matches the lowercase hostname `example.com`).

`LinkExtractor(allow_domains=...)` already lowercases domains (behavior asserted in `test_utils_url.py`). This PR aligns `OffsiteMiddleware` with that behavior by adding `.lower()` to the domain before `re.escape()`.

## Verification

```python
# Before: allowed_domains=["Example.COM"] → all requests filtered as offsite
# After: allowed_domains=["Example.COM"] → requests to example.com pass correctly
```

```python
FILES_STORE = "ftp://myhost.com/files"  # no port → AssertionError
```

## After


title: fix RobotsTxtMiddleware failing open for concurrent same-host requests
body:
## Description

Fixes a race in `RobotsTxtMiddleware` where `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True` silently **fails open** for the 2nd and later concurrent requests to a host, on the very first robots.txt fetch for that host.

### Root cause

When several requests to the same host are processed concurrently while the first robots.txt fetch is still in flight, `robot_parser()` stores a single shared `Deferred` in `self._parsers[netloc]` and every racing waiter converts it to an `asyncio` future via `Deferred.asFuture()` (inside `maybe_deferred_to_future`). Twisted's `maybeSucceed` callback implicitly returns `None` after setting *its own* future, so the `Deferred`'s chained result becomes `None` for the second and later waiters. Those waiters then observe `parser is None` and `process_request_2` treats `None` as "no parser available → allow the request", so disallowed paths are fetched instead of being blocked.

The reporter's instrumentation (issue #8297) observed this deterministically (4/4 runs).

### Fix

After awaiting the shared `Deferred`, re-read `self._parsers[netloc]`. `_parse_robots` / `_robots_error` always update that slot to the parsed parser (or `None` on error) **before** the `Deferred` fires, so it is the reliable source of truth for every waiter — independent of how many of them raced the same `asFuture()` future.

### Test

Added `test_robotstxt_concurrent_requests_same_host`: three concurrent same-host requests (one allowed + two disallowed) where one triggers the robots.txt download and the other two race it. It fails without the fix (the third waiter gets `None` and the disallowed request is not blocked) and passes with it.

Resolves #8297.

title: Drop deprecated CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP from the telnet console docs

The `slots` description in the Telnet Console docs offered
`CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP` as an alternative to `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN`

`.. setting::` directive defines it any more, so the `:setting:` role had no

single documented source of slot concurrency, per the contributing guide:
documentation about deprecated features must be removed as those features are
deprecated.

What I verified in the current tree:

- `scrapy/settings/__init__.py` raises `ScrapyDeprecationWarning` — "The
  CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP setting is deprecated, use
  CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN instead." — whenever the setting is read with
  a non-zero value.
- `scrapy/settings/default_settings.py` marks the
  `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP` attribute deprecated the same way.
- `scrapy/core/pqueues.py` rejects it outright: the memory queue raises
  `ValueError('"<queue>" does not support CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP')`.
- No `.. setting:: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP` directive exists anywhere in
  `docs/`, while `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` and `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN` are
  both still documented in `docs/topics/settings.rst`, so the remaining
  references keep resolving.

title: fix(cookies): process cookies from the Cookie request header
body:
## Summary

CookiesMiddleware dropped the `Cookie` request header, so cookies set through that header (directly on a request or through the `DEFAULT_REQUEST_HEADERS` setting) were never sent. The middleware now processes those cookies: they are merged into the `Cookie` header of their request, while cookies from the cookie jar (including the `Request.cookies` attribute and `Set-Cookie` response cookies) take precedence on name conflicts.

Header cookies are not stored in the cookie jar. Storing them was the behaviour reverted in #4823 because of #4717: a stale `Cookie` header copied onto a new request (e.g. by a redirect) overwrote fresher cookies set through `Set-Cookie`. Keeping header cookies request-local and letting the jar win restores the header support without reintroducing that bug.

## Changes

- `scrapy/downloadermiddlewares/cookies.py`: parse the `Cookie` header (UTF-8, falling back to Latin-1, last value wins for repeated names) and merge its cookies into the outgoing header after the jar sets its own, skipping names the jar already provides.
- `tests/test_downloadermiddleware_cookies.py`: remove the `xfail` markers from the three existing tests for this behaviour and add `test_cookie_header_not_stored_in_jar`, which covers both the request-local scope and the stale-header scenario from #4717.
- `docs/topics/cookies.rst`, `docs/topics/settings.rst`: replace the cautions saying `Cookie` header cookies are not handled with a description of the new behaviour.

## Tests

- `python -m pytest tests/test_downloadermiddleware_cookies.py -q` — 618 passed, 83 xfailed (pre-existing xfails for unrelated cookie domain limitations).
- `ruff check scrapy/downloadermiddlewares/cookies.py tests/test_downloadermiddleware_cookies.py` — all checks passed; `ruff format --check` on both files — already formatted.

Fixes #1992

title: Preserve robots.txt parser results for concurrent waiters
body:
## Motivation

With robots.txt obedience enabled, a disallowed URL is still downloaded when another request to the same host is already waiting on the first robots.txt lookup. The download succeeds and the page is passed to the spider.

Requests for one host all wait on a single Deferred stored in the per-host parser cache. robot_parser returned the value of awaiting that Deferred, and that await delivers the result to one callback, so every later waiter gets None and the middleware allows the download.

## What this changes

robot_parser still awaits the shared Deferred, then returns the parser already stored for that host, which is the parsed robots.txt or None if retrieval failed, and asserts the cache entry is no longer a Deferred. The two existing concurrent-request tests, on both reactors, now cover one allowed URL and two disallowed URLs and check that robots.txt is downloaded once. test_robotstxt_error_multiple_reqs and test_robotstxt_error_multiple_reqs_asyncio cover the same concurrency when the robots.txt download fails, with every waiter allowed through after that single attempt.

## How it was tested

Pytest -q tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py stopped while loading conftest and did not run any test.

Fixes #8297

title: Fix robots.txt enforcement failing open for multiple concurrent waiters (#8297)
body:
Resolves #8297.

### Description
As reported and discussed in #8297, when multiple concurrent requests to the same host wait on the shared `robots.txt` Deferred during initial fetch/parsing, `RobotsTxtMiddleware.robot_parser()` previously did:
```python
parser = self._parsers[netloc]
if isinstance(parser, Deferred):
    return await maybe_deferred_to_future(parser)
return parser
```
Under Twisted, `Deferred.asFuture()` attaches callbacks to the Deferred that do not return the result (`maybeSucceed` returns `None`), consuming the result for subsequent callbacks in the chain. Consequently, the first waiter received the parsed `RobotParser`, but subsequent concurrent waiters received `None`. Because `process_request_2()` treats `None` as "no parser available", all subsequent concurrent waiters bypassed robots.txt enforcement and were allowed to fetch forbidden paths.

### Solution
- Chain a dedicated per-waiter `Deferred` using `parser.addCallbacks(cb, eb)` where `cb` explicitly returns `result` and forwards it to the per-waiter Deferred before conversion to future.
- Added regression tests in `tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py` for both Twisted Deferreds and asyncio covering 3+ concurrent requests to ensure disallowed paths are strictly rejected with `IgnoreRequest`.

title: Fix fail-open robots.txt enforcement for concurrent requests to same host
body:
## Description
Fixes #8297

When `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True`, multiple concurrent requests targeting the same host before `robots.txt` has finished downloading share a single Twisted `Deferred` instance inside `RobotsTxtMiddleware.robot_parser()`.

In #6802, `robot_parser` was refactored to an async coroutine that awaited `maybe_deferred_to_future(parser)`. Because Twisted's `Deferred.asFuture()` consumes the Deferred's result without returning it (`maybeSucceed` sets the future's result and returns `None`), only the first concurrent waiter received the parsed `RobotParser` instance. All subsequent concurrent waiters received `None`.

In `RobotsTxtMiddleware.process_request_2(rp, request)`, `rp is None` was treated as "no parser available -> allow request", causing all subsequent concurrent requests to silently fail open and bypass robots exclusion rules even for disallowed paths.

## Solution
1. Restore per-waiter `Deferred` instances in `RobotsTxtMiddleware.robot_parser()`.
2. Register callback and errback handlers that forward the parsed result (`RobotParser | None` or `Failure`) to each waiter's private `Deferred` while returning the result so subsequent callbacks in Twisted's callback chain receive it unchanged.
3. Await each waiter's private Deferred via `maybe_deferred_to_future(d)`. This preserves proper result delivery to all concurrent waiters and prevents cancellation of one waiter from canceling the shared robots.txt download.

## Tests Added
- `test_robotstxt_multiple_reqs_forbidden`: Regression test with `DeferredList` confirming multiple concurrent disallowed requests are rejected with `IgnoreRequest`.
- `test_robotstxt_multiple_reqs_asyncio_forbidden`: Reproduction test under `asyncio.gather`.
- `test_robotstxt_error_multiple_reqs`: Error path regression test when robots.txt fails to download.
- `test_robotstxt_subsequent_requests_cached_parser`: Verifies cached parser reuse after initial resolution.
- `test_robotstxt_multiple_hosts_concurrency`: Verifies multi-host concurrent isolation.
- `test_robotstxt_cancellation_isolation`: Verifies that canceling one waiter does not cancel the shared download.
- `test_robotstxt_concurrent_forbidden_stats`: Verifies stats counters and download deduplication.
- `TestRobotsTxtMiddlewareWithPythonRobotParser`: Verifies all behaviors against `PythonRobotParser` backend.

body:

- [x] I have read the [contributing guide](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html) and [set up pre-commit](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html#pre-commit).

## What

In `RobotsTxtMiddleware.robot_parser()`, after awaiting the shared per-host `Deferred`, re-read the authoritative value from `self._parsers[netloc]` instead of using the awaited value:

```python
parser = self._parsers[netloc]
if isinstance(parser, Deferred):
    await maybe_deferred_to_future(parser)
    parser = self._parsers[netloc]
    assert not isinstance(parser, Deferred)
return parser
```

Two regression tests are added to `tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py`, covering the concurrent + disallowed combination (the existing concurrent tests only used allowed URLs).

## Why

All waiters for the same host share one `Deferred` (#6802 simplified this from per-waiter Deferreds), and its result is consumed by the first waiter:

- under the asyncio reactor, `maybe_deferred_to_future()` resolves to `Deferred.asFuture()` (`scrapy/utils/defer.py`), which hands the result to the first waiter and `None` to later ones;
- under the non-asyncio reactor, the raw `Deferred` is returned and later waiters receive `None` through the Twisted callback chain the same way.

`process_request_2()` treats `None` as "no parser available" and allows the request (`scrapy/downloadermiddlewares/robotstxt.py`), so with `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True` every same-host request after the first concurrent one silently bypasses robots.txt enforcement (fail-open).

Re-reading `self._parsers[netloc]` after the await is authoritative for every waiter, because both writers update the dict *before* firing the Deferred: `_parse_robots()` and `_robots_error()`. The error path keeps its existing semantics (parser `None` → request proceeds), so there is no behavior change beyond the bug fix. Root cause confirmed by @wRAR in #8297 (introduced by #6802).

Note: #8307 proposed the same minimal fix for the asyncio path but was auto-closed by the unattended-PR guard and is inactive. This PR additionally covers the non-asyncio reactor, where the same fail-open occurs and which was verified locally (below).

## How I verified

Environment: Python 3.13.12, Twisted 26.4.0, pytest 9.1.1, `pip install -e .` from this branch.

1. Reproduction script: 3 concurrent `process_request()` calls against a robots.txt that disallows `/admin/`, asserting `["ALLOWED", "IGNORED", "IGNORED"]`:
   - on master it fails under **both** `--reactor=asyncio` and `--reactor=default`: one of the disallowed requests comes back ALLOWED, e.g. `{'allowed': 'ALLOWED', 'admin/one': 'IGNORED', 'admin/two': 'ALLOWED'}`;
   - with this change it passes under both reactors.
2. `pytest tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py -q`:
   - master: `16 passed, 16 skipped`;
   - with this change: `18 passed, 18 skipped` (`--reactor=asyncio`, CI default) and `16 passed, 20 skipped` (`--reactor=default`, where the new `only_asyncio` tests are skipped and the new `DeferredList`-based test runs and passes).
3. The new tests fail without the fix and pass with it: `pytest tests/test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py -q -k disallowed` → 2 failed on master (asyncio reactor; under `--reactor=default` the non-asyncio variant fails too), all pass with this change.
4. `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `mypy scrapy/downloadermiddlewares/robotstxt.py` are clean; the full robotstxt suite was run 5 times per reactor with no flakes.

title: fix(robotstxt): deliver parsed parser to all concurrent waiters
body:
## Summary

Fixes #8297: concurrent requests to the same host could silently bypass `robots.txt` enforcement.

## Root cause

Concurrent same-host requests share a single Twisted `Deferred` for the robots.txt fetch/parse in `RobotsTxtMiddleware.robot_parser()`. Each waiter awaited it through `maybe_deferred_to_future()`, which calls `Deferred.asFuture()`.

Twisted's `asFuture()` *consumes* the Deferred's result (see its docstring: "converting a Deferred to a Future consumes both its result and its errors"). So only the **first** waiter received the parsed parser; every additional waiter received `None`. `process_request_2()` treats `None` as "no parser available", so those requests **failed open** and bypassed `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY`.

A minimal reproduction confirms the behavior — with three concurrent requests (one allowed, two disallowed), the second disallowed request returned `ALLOWED`:

```
ALLOWED  http://site.local/allowed
BLOCKED  http://site.local/private/a.html
ALLOWED  http://site.local/private/b.html   # wrong: should be BLOCKED
```

## Change

In `robot_parser()`, after awaiting the shared `Deferred`, read the final value back from `self._parsers[netloc]` instead of trusting the (consumed) `asFuture()` result:

```python
parser = self._parsers[netloc]
if isinstance(parser, Deferred):
    await maybe_deferred_to_future(parser)
    parser = self._parsers[netloc]
return parser
```

Every concurrent waiter now receives the actual `RobotParser` (or `None` on error), restoring correct allow/deny decisions.

## Tests

Added `test_robotstxt_multiple_reqs_asyncio_disallowed`, which races one allowed and two disallowed requests against the same host and asserts the disallowed ones are both blocked.

- Before the fix the test fails with `[False, True, False]`; after the fix it passes with `[False, True, True]`.
- Full `test_downloadermiddleware_robotstxt.py` suite: **17 passed, 17 skipped** (`--reactor asyncio`).
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on both changed files.

title: Add COMPRESSION_PRESERVE_CONTENT_ENCODING setting
body:
Resolves #1988.

- [x] I have read the [contributing guide](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html) and [set up pre-commit](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html#pre-commit).

**Summary**

`HttpCompressionMiddleware` currently removes decoded encodings from the `Content-Encoding` header, so a spider cannot see the original response headers of a fully decompressed response (as reported in #1988).

This PR adds a `COMPRESSION_PRESERVE_CONTENT_ENCODING` setting (default `False`, so the current behavior is unchanged). When enabled, the original `Content-Encoding` header is restored in fully decompressed responses, and a `"decompressed"` flag is added to `response.flags` so consumers can tell that the body is no longer compressed.

The header is restored only after `responsetypes` has classified the response, because `responsetypes.from_content_type()` treats the presence of `Content-Encoding` as a sign of a compressed body; this way response class guessing (e.g. `HtmlResponse` vs plain `Response`) still works as before.

Partially decoded responses (those with unsupported encodings left) keep the current header handling. I have intentionally left the `scrapy startproject` settings template unchanged (kmike's original suggestion included enabling this in newly generated projects) — happy to add that if preferred.

**Tests**

- Added `test_process_response_gzip_preserve_content_encoding` verifying that with the setting enabled the original header is preserved, the `"decompressed"` flag is set, and the response is still classified as `HtmlResponse`.
- Extended `test_process_response_gzip` to also assert that no flag is added when the setting is disabled (default).
- `pytest tests/test_downloadermiddleware_httpcompression.py`: 65 passed.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on the changed files.

title: Fix FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS silently dropping (name, output) pair entries
body:
## `FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS` silently drops every `(name, output)` pair entry

### Description

In `BaseItemExporter.get_serialized_fields`, the branch that filters a non-`Mapping` `fields_to_export` down to populated fields tested the **whole list entry** against the item:

```python
field_iter = (x for x in self.fields_to_export if x in item)
```

But the loop immediately below explicitly supports two entry shapes:

```python
for field_name in field_iter:
    if isinstance(field_name, str):
        item_field, output_field = field_name, field_name
    else:
        item_field, output_field = field_name      # (item_field, output_field) pair
```

So when an entry is a pair, `x` is the tuple `("field1", "Field 1")`, and `"('field1', 'Field 1')" in item` is a lookup of a *tuple key* that no item can have. **Every pair entry is silently dropped and the item exports as empty.**

### Why it's wrong, not a design choice

- The code path explicitly exists to support pair entries — that is what the `else: item_field, output_field = field_name` unpack is for.
- The `Mapping` branch ten lines above (line 115) does it correctly: `for x, y in self.fields_to_export.items() if x in item` tests the **key**. The two branches implement identical semantics; only the list one is wrong.
- `BaseSettings.getdictorlist`, the documented parser for `FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS`, has explicitly supported tuple values since gh:6011 (`docs/news/2.x.rst:1602`: *"`BaseSettings.getdictorlist`, used to parse `FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS`, now handles tuple values"*). A value of `(("field1", "Field 1"),)` is a first-class documented input, and it is broken.
- The identical `export_empty_fields=True` configuration works, which proves the *filter* is at fault, not the data.

### Impact: silent data loss

`JsonLinesItemExporter` writes `{}`; `XmlItemExporter` writes `<item></item>`. The user asks for fields, gets none, and nothing errors. The list-of-lists form — what `json.loads` produces for `-s FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS='[["a","A"]]'` — was worse: it raised `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.

### Reproduction (real output, unmodified HEAD)

```
expected with output renaming:
dict (rename)                {"Field 1": "v1", "Field 2": "v2"}
list of str                  {"field1": "v1", "field2": "v2"}

actual with the same fields as (name, output) pairs:
dict (rename)                {"Field 1": "v1", "Field 2": "v2"}
list of tuple (rename)       {}

only `export_empty_fields=True` makes the tuple form work:
list of tuple + empty        {"Field 1": "v1", "Field 2": "v2"}

and the FEED_EXPORT_FIELDS setting path:
setting value -> [('field1', 'Field 1'), ('field2', 'Field 2')]
from setting                 {}
```

and through the real setting path the list-of-lists form crashed outright:

```
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
  scrapy/exporters.py:120 in <genexpr>: field_iter = (x for x in self.fields_to_export if x in item)
```

### The fix

```python
# A non-Mapping iterable can contain (item_field, output_field) pairs,
# so the item field, and not the whole entry, is what must be looked
# up in the item.
field_iter = (
    x
    for x in self.fields_to_export
    if (x if isinstance(x, str) else x[0]) in item
)
```

## Tests

`test_fields_to_export_pairs` added to `TestBaseItemExporter` in `tests/test_exporters.py`, which is inherited by all 17 exporter test classes. Parametrized per `AGENTS.md`, covering the str list, tuple pairs, list pairs, dict, multi-field ordering, and missing-field filtering.

- Before the fix: **68 failed, 68 passed** — the 68 failures are exactly the pair-form cases across every exporter class, while the string-list and dict forms passed, isolating the defect to the pair path. After: **136 passed**.
- `tests/test_exporters.py` → **324 passed**.
- No regressions nearby: `tests/test_feedexport.py tests/test_settings` → 175 passed, 1 xfailed; `tests/test_feedexport_postprocess.py tests/test_feedexport_uri_params.py tests/test_item.py` → 49 passed.
- `ruff check` clean, `ruff format` applied.

I checked the open issues and PRs: nothing covers this. The nearest exporter issues are #3888 (nested items) and #4777 (`CsvItemExporter` dynamic headers), both unrelated.

One real neighbouring defect I deliberately left out of scope: `url_is_from_any_domain` compares `netloc`, so a port or credentials defeat matching (`http://a.example.com:8080/` misses `example.com`) — but `tests/test_utils_url.py:31-33` **asserts** that behaviour, so fixing it is a breaking change, not a bug fix.

Note the repo's `close-spam-prs.yml` workflow auto-closes PRs whose author activity suggests unsupervised LLM use; this PR is reviewed and the change is small and test-backed, but I wanted it on the record.

title: Make closing the spider stop the engine, other state transition fixes
body:
Next part of #6916, that solves most of it.

There are multiple behavior changes for many of the involved methods here, but that was necessary to avoid several classes of deadlocks. There are future improvements possible (for behavior existing in master) regarding stuff like waiting for completion of the same transition from multiple callers.

This also makes `engine.state` and its type, `EngineState`, public. I thought about dropping `engine.running` or at least removing its usages from the Scrapy code itself, but that doesn't seem to have benefits.

The differences between `close_async()` vs `stop_async()` vs `close_spider_async()` (which I already noted in #6916) may now be even more confusing than before, and we may want to drop some of them later, but all of them are public and must have many callers so it's for later at best.

The most controversial sounding change, that closing the spider means stopping the engine, already existed before when using `Crawler`, via `_spider_closed_callback()`. The asymmetrical order of signals (`spider_opened → engine_started → spider_closed → engine_stopped`) looks weird but this is how it was before (#1523, and the reasons are likely just historical but I would hesitate to change it), and the low-level justification is "you need to open the spider before starting the engine", "closing the spider stops the engine as the final step" and "calling `stop()` directly still called `close_spider()` and only then sent `engine_stopped`".

title: Fix file store modification timestamps
body:
S3 and GCS modification datetimes were reinterpreted in the host timezone, while FTP MDTM calendar values were treated as Unix timestamps, which could make `FilesPipeline` cache ages incorrect.

This converts cloud datetimes directly and parses FTP MDTM values as UTC, with regression coverage for offset-aware and fractional timestamps.

Validation:

- `tox -e extra-deps -- tests/test_pipeline_files.py -q`
- `pre-commit run --all-files`
- mypy and pylint on the changed files

title: Scan the whole response for base URL and meta refresh on w3lib 2.5.0+
body:
Resolves #3017.

We should also make a decision on what we want to do:
- Do we keep the current cap, change it or lift it?
- Do we use different caps for base URL and meta refresh?
- Do we allow users to override the cap? (if we do, for setting names we could use `HTML_MAX_SCAN` if 1 setting or `BASE_URL_MAX_SCAN` and `METAREFRESH_MAX_SCAN` if 2)

I had an LLM download the homepage of ~1k websites popular in terms of web scraping, plus listing pages and details pages for some of them, and gather data on what different caps would buy us, with w3lib 2.5.0, in terms of performance and coverage:

> I pulled data for this instead of guessing: 1512 pages from 906 of the top 1000 domains by usage, […], measuring where `<base href>` and the meta refresh tag actually sit in `response.text`.
>
> […]
>
> The two tags behave nothing alike, which I think settles it in favor of two separate settings:
>
> ```
> <base href>      present on   23/1512 pages (1.5%)     meta refresh   present on   64/1512 pages (4.2%)
>   p50    0.1 KB                                          p50    2.5 KB
>   p75    2.2 KB                                          p75   10.2 KB
>   p90    6.5 KB                                          p90  128.5 KB
>   p100 100.3 KB                                          p100 581.8 KB
>
> coverage by cap                                        coverage by cap
>    4 KB   82.6%     32 KB   91.3%                         4 KB   56.2%     32 KB   81.2%
>    8 KB   91.3%    128 KB  100.0%                         8 KB   75.0%    128 KB   89.1%
>   16 KB   91.3%    256 KB  100.0%                        16 KB   78.1%    256 KB   93.8%
> ```
>
> `<base href>` is rare and sits at the very top, so 8 KB gets 91% of it. A meta refresh can be anywhere, and our current 4096 misses 44% of them, i.e. about 1.8% of all pages have a meta refresh we silently ignore. That is a redirect the crawl never follows.
>
> Mean cost per response over the same corpus, from the measured linear scan rates:
>
> ```
>        cap    get_base_url    get_meta_refresh
>       4096       0.0013 ms         0.0034 ms
>       8192       0.0025 ms         0.0067 ms
>      32768       0.0100 ms         0.0266 ms
>     131072       0.0375 ms         0.0998 ms
>  unlimited       0.1612 ms         0.4294 ms
> ```
>
> I would default both to `0`, no limit, and leave the settings as the escape hatch for whoever cares about the 0.59 ms. Against a selector build on a 500 KB page that is single digit percent, and it is the only default that is right every time. [Mind that the LLM here has most likely been biased by my personal preference for correctness over performance]
>
> If we would rather cap by default, the knee points are 8192 for the base URL and 131072 for the meta refresh. Anything between 8 KB and 128 KB for the meta refresh pays for coverage it does not get, the curve is almost flat there.
>
> Two caveats. The `<base href>` numbers rest on 23 pages, so that tail is not really characterized, the p95 of 100 KB is one or two pages. And the corpus is 60% home pages, since my link heuristics only found a listing page for 44% of the domains and a detail page for 17%.
